title: Clicking Joints
meta_title: Clicking Joints: When Is It Arthritis and When Is It Normal?

content:
Clicking, cracking or popping joints are very common and are usually harmless if there is no pain or swelling. The noise often comes from gas bubbles in joint fluid or tendons moving over bone. Grinding or crunching with pain, called crepitus, can be a sign of osteoarthritis. See your GP or physiotherapist if clicking comes with pain, swelling, locking or the joint giving way.

Why joints make noises

  • gas bubbles: joints are surrounded by fluid that contains dissolved gases. Stretching the joint can release a bubble with a pop, as when cracking knuckles. It takes time to build up again, so it usually cannot be repeated straight away.
  • tendons and ligaments can snap over bony areas as you move, especially at the hip, knee and shoulder
  • roughened joint surfaces can create a grinding or crunching feeling, common in osteoarthritis
  • cartilage tears in the knee can cause clicking with catching or locking

Usually nothing to worry about

Clicking is likely to be harmless if:

  • there is no pain
  • there is no swelling
  • the joint moves normally and does not lock or give way
  • it has been happening for a long time without change

Painless clicking does not mean you are developing arthritis. Many people with noisy knees never develop osteoarthritis.

When it might be arthritis

Osteoarthritis can cause:

  • a grating or crunching feeling or sound when moving the joint
  • pain that is worse with activity and eases with rest
  • short-lived stiffness after resting or in the morning
  • swelling, sometimes with knobbly finger joints

It is most common in knees, hips, hands and the spine, mainly after 45.

Other causes to consider

  • kneecap pain (patellofemoral pain): clicking at the front of the knee with pain on stairs, squatting or after sitting
  • meniscus (cartilage) tear: clicking with the knee catching, locking or giving way, often after a twisting injury
  • hypermobility: very flexible joints often click and can be prone to aches and sprains
  • snapping hip: a tendon flicking over the hip bone, usually painless
  • shoulder problems: clicking with pain when lifting the arm

What helps

If clicking is painless, you do not need to do anything. If there is mild pain:

  • strengthen the muscles around the joint. For knees, try sit to stands, step-ups and straight-leg raises.
  • stay active with low-impact activities such as walking, swimming or cycling
  • manage your weight to reduce load on knees and hips
  • use heat or cold for short-term relief
  • check your footwear for good cushioning and support

Many areas let you self-refer to NHS physiotherapy.

When to see a GP or physiotherapist

  • clicking comes with pain that does not improve after a few weeks
  • the joint is swollen, warm or stiff
  • the joint locks, catches or gives way
  • clicking started after an injury
  • you cannot move the joint fully

Your GP or physiotherapist will examine the joint and may suggest exercises, or refer you for imaging if a cartilage or ligament injury is suspected. Osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without an X-ray.

Should I stop cracking my knuckles?

There is no good evidence that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis. If it is painless, it is harmless, though you may want to stop if it bothers others. If cracking any joint becomes painful, get it checked.

Clicking and exercise

Many people worry that exercise will make a noisy joint worse. If clicking is painless, it is safe to carry on. If an exercise causes pain as well as clicking, change it, for example by reducing how deep you bend the knee, rather than stopping exercise altogether. Strengthening the surrounding muscles often reduces clicking over time.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
